To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the human ADH gene is expressed at different levels in different tissues, that the cis-acting elements of this promoter are occupied to different extents in different tissues, and that the occupancy of these sites is correlated with the expression of the gene in these tissues.

the human alcohol dehydroganse gene ADH2, expressed at high levels liver, at lower level in kidney, and not in spleen, is regulated by multiple transcription factors, which bind to specific cis-acting elements.

(i) the ADH2 gene is expressed in liver, kidney, and other tissues, but not in spleen; (ii) the proximal 300 bp of the AD H2 promoter contain several cis-acting sequences, which differ markedly in occupancy among different tissues; (iii) the promoter is active in H4I I E-C3 cells (a rat hepatoma) and HeLa cells, which express high levels of C/EBPs, but inactive in CV-1
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of gene expression in the adult human liver, and in particular with the transcriptional control of alcohol metabolism.
the regulation of gene expression in the liver and the kidney, two tissues with distinct functions and with different responses to toxic chemicals.
the molecular mechanisms of tissue-specific gene expression, and the role of transcription factors in the expression of alcohol dehydrogenases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the expression of the ADH 2 gene is tissue-specific and that this is due to the differential occupancy of the cis-acting elements by transcription factors in the different tissues.

the ADH2 gene is expressed at high level in the liver and in the kidney, and is also expressed in the pancreas, the adrenal gland, the testes, and the ovary, but at a much lower level, and that this expression is under the regulation of a complex regulatory region.
the expression of the ADH-2 gene is regulated in a tissue-specific manner by the combined action of multiple cis-acting elements that bind a variety of transcriptional factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ADH2 gene has a complex promoter region, with multiple sites for transcription factors that are differentially occupied in various cells, and that this complexity is required for the cell-specific expression of ADH.

the expression of ADH 2 in liver is controlled by the binding of liver-enriched transcriptional factors, including HNF-3, C/EBP, and CTF/NF-1, to specific cis-acting elements within its promoter, and that these factors act in a cooperative manner to stimulate transcription.
the ADH2 gene is regulated in a tissue-specific manner by a complex combination of positive and negative cis-acting elements and by specific transcription factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single cis-acting sequence can have different effects in different cells.
the ADH2 gene is regulated by different transcription factors and that the relative importance of these factors is cell type-specific.
the ADH2 gene promoter has multiple regulatory elements that are important in different cell lines.
